questions.q: Which four attributes define a ledger, as covered in this lesson?
options: Chart of Accounts, calendar, currency, and accounting method
Business unit, supplier list, customer list, and tax rate
Only the accounting method; the other three are optional
Chart of Accounts, calendar, business unit, and supporting reference
questions.explain: A ledger is defined by a Chart of Accounts, a calendar, a currency, and an accounting method; the accounting method is this course's focus.

questions.q: At what level is the Subledger Accounting Method assignment made?
options: At the individual journal line level
At the business unit level, separately for each business unit
At the ledger level, not the business unit level
At the supplier level
questions.explain: The accounting method is one of a ledger's core attributes; multiple business units sharing a ledger all use that ledger's one assigned method.

questions.q: Why does the accounting method assignment belong at the ledger level rather than the business unit level?
options: Because business units cannot process any transactions
Because the ledger is what actually gets debited and credited, and holds the Chart of Accounts and trial balance, while a business unit is mainly an operational/security construct
Because Oracle has no concept of business units
Because accounting methods only apply to Receivables
questions.explain: Journal entries and the trial balance live at the ledger level, which is why the accounting method — which determines how journal entries are built — is assigned there.

questions.q: Can a primary ledger and a secondary ledger recording the same transactions use different accounting methods?
options: No, every ledger in a company must share the exact same accounting method
Yes — each ledger is defined independently and can carry its own accounting method, such as one built for local GAAP and another for IFRS
Only secondary ledgers are allowed to have an accounting method at all
This is only possible if the two ledgers share a Chart of Accounts
questions.explain: Primary and secondary ledgers are defined independently and can each use a different accounting method for the same underlying transactions.

questions.q: What is the practical consequence of changing the accounting method assigned to a ledger?
options: Nothing changes; the assignment is purely informational
It changes how every future transaction for that ledger, across every subledger application, gets accounted, which is why it is a carefully controlled change
It only affects Fixed Assets, never any other subledger
It immediately deletes all historical journal entries
questions.explain: Because the accounting method determines how every subledger's events are processed into journal entries for that ledger, changing it is a significant, carefully controlled action.
